abstract: We report the first genome-wide ancient DNA data from a medieval population in the territory of the modern Republic of Karelia, Russia: 1240K capture data for 22 individuals from the Kondopoga cemetery on Lake Onega, a churchyard used from the 12th to the 19th century. Combining relatedness estimates, autosomal and X-chromosomal identity-by-descent, uniparental lineages, burial position and archaeological dating, we place eight individuals in a single pedigree spanning five generations, anchored on a founding couple buried in the highest part of the cemetery. Identity-by-descent links almost all the remaining individuals to that couple, indicating that the sample is not a cross-section of a local population but a single kindred, which is the object of this study. Within it, the founding males paternal lineage recurs from the 12th-13th to the 16th century, mitochondrial lineages differ between individuals of the same generation, and autosomal ancestry shifts between generations rather than between archaeological phases. The ancestry of the founders is closest to populations from northwestern Rus and the eastern Baltic, while the Uralic-related ancestry entering the pedigree is best modelled using present-day Finnic groups of the region. The family was patrilineal, and its profile was reshaped by the women who married into it.
